desc:
Each job is given as [start, end, profit] and occupies the time interval from start to end. You can do only one job at a time. Two chosen jobs are compatible if one ends no later than the other starts: a job that ends at time t may be followed by a job that starts at time t.

Return the maximum total profit of a set of pairwise compatible jobs (the empty set has profit 0).
hints: A greedy choice (earliest end, highest profit) fails here because profits differ. Think of a DP over jobs ordered by end time.
Sort jobs by end time. Let dp[i] be the best profit using only the first i jobs of that order. Either skip job i, or take it together with the best result among jobs that finish by its start.
The number of jobs that end at or before start of job i is an upper-bound search in the sorted array of end times. Then dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[that count] + profit).
editorial: Sort the jobs by end time and let ends be the sorted end times. Define dp[i] as the best profit using only the first i jobs in this order (dp[0] = 0). For job number i (1-based) there are two choices: skip it, giving dp[i - 1]; or take it, which allows exactly those earlier jobs that end at or before its start. Because the list is sorted by end, those jobs are a prefix of it, and the prefix length is bisect_right(ends, start) (jobs ending exactly at start are allowed). The value is dp[prefix] + profit.

The prefix can be found only among the jobs before i; since the job itself has end > start, the upper bound is never beyond i - 1, so the lookup is safe. Sorting takes O(n log n), and the n binary searches another O(n log n). The result is dp[n]. The profits sum to at most 1,200 × 10,000, so there is no overflow.
solution:
from bisect import bisect_right

def maxJobProfit(jobs):
    jobs = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[1])
    ends = [j[1] for j in jobs]
    dp = [0] * (len(jobs) + 1)
    for i, (s, e, w) in enumerate(jobs, 1):
        k = bisect_right(ends, s)
        dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1], dp[k] + w)
    return dp[-1]
